title: The FAT write path and fsck
summary: The write path is the best-argued subsystem in the tree. One commit order (data, FAT flush, entry, free, flush) holds in every mutator: write, mkdir, delete, rmdir, rmtree, truncate, append-grow, held streams, fsck repairs and defrag moves. Replace is shadowed, so a power cut never costs the user's bytes, which DOS cannot claim. Every LBA and chain walk is bounded against a hostile disk. The defects are at the edges the prose did not reach. A hostile FileSize faults two unguarded divides (the truncate arm has the guard; its siblings do not). Since the whole-FAT snapshot became a window, a failed write on multi-window FAT16 can turn walked free space into permanent lost clusters (dskw_refat's header accepts lost clusters; a disk-full failure makes that most of the free space). An unreadable FAT window reports 'Disk full', the exact misreport the allocator's header forbids. The UI-task rule is still enforced by nothing. On design, the whole-file model's foreknowledge of size is unused: no up-front FERR_FULL, no contiguous allocation. Folders never grow (DOS 2.0 did). The compression hint lives in three dirent bytes that NT, Linux, macOS and OS/2 all interpret, so every packed file on every shipped disk lists in lower case on a modern host. fsck's model (kernel image, package-owned state, write generation, ordered repairs, moves only into free space) is sound and worth copying; its issues are one parse bug and stale docs. Most fixes are 0-25 bytes of .cold; the larger items (folder growth ~90, contiguous allocation ~70) are optional rethinks. A large share of SPEC 18.4's own text (fmv_gneed, the remount, the whole-FAT snapshot, refat's disk_read, 'no append or seek') describes a kernel several passes old.

strengths.title: Shadow replace with one commit point
strengths.evidence: kernel/diskw.inc:1576-1597 (dskw_wbody: old chain held until the entry write, freed by dskw_relold after)
strengths.why: DOS truncates in place on create-over-existing, so a crash there loses both versions; here a crash costs at most lost clusters.

strengths.title: One commit order everywhere, argued at each site
strengths.evidence: mkdir :666-743, delete/rmdir :906-913, truncate :3838-3879, grow .seal :4007-4057, fsck repairs fsck.inc:1704-1724, moves :3105-3191
strengths.why: The same 'worst case is lost clusters' argument can be checked locally at every mutator.

strengths.title: Hostile-disk discipline
strengths.evidence: dsk_clus2lba_x/dskw_clok on every cluster; dskw_free_chain bounded by maxclus (:4801-4816); DSK_DIRW_MAX on directory walks; dskw_size32 refusal before I/O
strengths.why: A corrupt or hostile volume can make an operation fail but cannot steer a write outside the volume.

strengths.title: Allocation marks before returning and separates full from I/O failure
strengths.why: A half-built chain can never hand the same cluster out twice.

strengths.title: Cross-cluster runs capped by DMA page from the advancing segment; zero-filled staged tail
strengths.why: The 8237 page bug is unreachable from any caller buffer, and a contiguous file is one int 13h per track.

strengths.title: Entry taken while in hand; entry store always re-reads before patching
strengths.why: Saves a revolution per open, and a stale dsk_secbuf can never resurrect neighbouring entries.

strengths.title: Protection tiers as one routine; virtual read-only bit only in the staged copy
strengths.why: A mounted image cannot be destroyed, and nothing is written to the disk to say so.

strengths.title: Iterative rmtree using on-disk '..' with emptiness re-checked at every removal
strengths.why: No stack depth on 384-byte task stacks, and disagreeing scans give a refusal rather than a lost subtree.

strengths.title: fsck's stateless-kernel, generation-checked, bounded-step model
strengths.evidence: fsck.inc:20-22, fsk_step :770-787, fsk_move/fsk_link only into free clusters, fsk_foldok re-asked before link
strengths.why: It checks and defragments a live desktop safely and stops cleanly when the disk moves under it, where DOS CHKDSK /F and DEFRAG need an idle machine. This is the pattern for any long-running kernel service.

strengths.title: Formatter probe separates medium from drive; reach test writes a marker
strengths.why: It is the honest answer to the 40-track-disk-in-80-track-drive trap, and makes every test a positive one.

findings.title: Hostile FileSize faults two unguarded divides (append/write-at and READ_AT)
findings.detail: dskw_wabody .div divides the offset by the cluster size with no high-word check. On APPEND the offset is the entry's size, accepted whenever it is cluster-aligned. dskw_read_at_x divides the caller's offset, bounded only by the entry's size. With a 512-byte cluster, a high word of 512 or more (offset of 32MB or more) overflows the quotient. Examples: an entry claiming 0x02000000 bytes on a floppy, then OSAPI_FILE_APPEND; or a DOS program lseeking past 32MB in such a file, since DOS.O88's window is READ_AT. No INT 0 handler exists in the tree. On an 8088 with the BIOS dummy, execution continues with garbage. On a 286+ the div re-executes forever. A DOS program's runtime INT 0 hook would run in kernel context. The truncate arm already has the guard, and SPEC 18.4.7.5 states the reason. Both divides are assembled on BOTH kernels (neither is under an %ifdef).
evidence: kernel/diskw.inc:3128-3134 offset bounded only by entry size
kernel/diskw.inc:3850-3851 truncate's guard cmp dx,bx / jae .corrupt
SPEC.md 18.4.7.5 'the divide would otherwise fault inside the file layer'
findings.recommendation: Before each div add 'cmp dx, <bytes per cluster> / jae <FERR_IO arm>' (.jcor is in reach in wabody; READ_AT needs stc before .rdend). Fix the 'offset is under 33MB (SPEC.md 18.7)' comments in the same edit.
findings.bytes_est: about +4 at wabody's div and +6-8 at READ_AT's (cmp dx,[dwr_clb] / jae + an arm), .cold resident, on BOTH kernels
findings.verify_note: Confirmed both divides unguarded (diskw.inc:3930-3932, 3168-3170) and truncate's guard at 3850-3851; nothing earlier bounds the entry's size high word. Correction: the READ_AT div and the wabody div are both outside any KERN_SMALL %ifdef, so kern_small needs both guards too; the '+11 kern_big, +4 kern_small' split was wrong.

findings.title: Failed write on multi-window FAT16 leaks the half-built chain the window evictions flushed
findings.detail: The plain rollback arms only call dskw_refat, which is an invalidate with no I/O. dskw_alloc's FAT16 scan and dskw_setfat's links move the FAT window, and dsk_fat_window flushes before it evicts, so the chain built so far reaches the disk as an orphan. On FERR_FULL the write has walked every free cluster, so the volume stays 'full' until a System Check repair, even after the user deletes the file they were saving. FAT12 floppies (whole window) are immune. The HELD arm already frees its own sub-chain before flushing, and its comment names exactly this leak ('on a DISK FULL, every free cluster the volume had left'). dskw_refat's header accepts lost clusters as the price of the window; the disk-full case is what makes that price the whole free space.
evidence: kernel/diskw.inc:5008-5012 refat header admits an eviction may already have flushed part of the chain
kernel/diskw.inc:4069-4087 HELD rollback frees its own sub-chain first
findings.recommendation: In both plain arms: mov ax,[dskw_first] / call dskw_free_chain / call dskw_flush_x, and dskw_refat only if that flush fails. The chain is linked in RAM, so the walk frees exactly what was built.
findings.verify_note: Confirmed: wdata sets [dskw_first] at the first allocation (:1671-1673), every allocation is EOC-marked before use, and in wabody the link to the file's last cluster happens only at .link after the sub-chain flush (:4024-4031), so freeing from [dskw_first] on .rbdrop frees exactly the unlinked sub-chain. Not in ABI-BREAK-LIST or KERNEL-BYTE-QUEUE.

findings.title: Unreadable FAT window reads as 'Disk full', after a per-cluster retry storm
findings.detail: dskw_alloc .one treats a CF from dsk_next_clus_x as 'used' and goes on. The rover keeps candidates in range, so that CF can only be I/O. The FAT16 .scan falls back to .one on the same load failure and asks again for the next cluster. With both FAT copies unreadable, every candidate costs a failed load (three attempts plus resets), and the answer is AX=0 CF=1, which every caller maps to FERR_FULL. That is exactly the misreport the routine's header says it exists to prevent.
evidence: kernel/diskw.inc:4680-4684 header: an I/O error must not say 'Disk full'
findings.recommendation: In .one, jc to 'pop ax / stc / jmp .iofail' so the answer is 0FFFFh, the I/O failure.
findings.verify_note: Confirmed: dsk_next_clus_x (disk.inc:6537-6573) sets CF only for a cluster outside [2,maxclus] or a failed dsk_fat_ofs_x; .try wraps the candidate into range first, so CF in .one is I/O. It decodes no EOC, so CF never means 'end mark'.

findings.title: The UI-task-only rule for every file cell is enforced by nothing
findings.detail: Every body shares .bss scratch (dskw_raw, dskw_n83, dsk_secbuf, the dirty range), and the N-stub stages names into one api_name/api_name2 pair. A package worker calling a file cell while the UI task is inside one cross-links the FAT silently. SPEC 18.4 itself says 'The kernel cannot enforce this'. The kernel already tests 'am I the UI task' with cmp byte [sch_cur],0 in several places. Prior art: DOS made re-entry detectable (InDOS); the Mac File Manager serialized async calls through a queue. A refusal is enough here.
evidence: SPEC.md 18.4 Context paragraph 'an author rule with nothing behind it'
kernel/memory.inc:955, kernel/instance.inc:2203, kernel/toast.inc:407 the existing sch_cur==0 test
findings.recommendation: Put cmp byte [sch_cur],0 / jne refuse (FERR_NODISK) once in the file cells' N-stub, or in dskw_mounted/dskw_gate, which every body passes. First confirm that kerndos, HIBER and drivers never call the bodies off task 0 - DOS.O88 owns a worker (dvw_start, apps/dos/dos.asm:2010), so its file calls must be shown to run on task 0 before the refusal lands.
findings.prior_art: MS-DOS InDOS flag (detect re-entry); Mac File Manager async queue (serialize)
findings.verify_note: Confirmed: SPEC.md:34500-34501 says it verbatim and diskw.inc:27-31 agrees; sch_cur==0 tests exist at memory.inc:955/4704, instance.inc:2203, toast.inc:407, wm.inc:11763. Added the DOS worker as the caller to clear first.

findings.title: A failed FAT flush keeps its dirt, which dsk_fatw_park may later write to another disk
findings.detail: dskw_flush_x's .ioerr skips .reset, so the dirty range survives a failed write. dskw_relold flushes 'EITHER WAY' precisely because dirt carried across a media change lands on the next disk's FAT. dsk_fatw_park flushes outgoing dirt at the top of the next mount, before it can know a floppy was swapped. So a post-commit flush failure, then a swap, then a volume switch, writes old FAT sectors onto the new disk.
findings.recommendation: .ioerr: call dskw_ioerr / call dskw_refat (drop range and window). A post-commit failure then costs lost clusters, which the order already accepts. Check the held-stream path first: a HELD call's flush failure already poisons the stream (dws_hlose), so dropping the window there loses nothing new.
findings.verify_note: Confirmed: .ioerr (diskw.inc:4989) jumps to .out past .reset; .stale (:4977-4987) does reach .reset. disk.inc:5794-5799 flushes dirt in park with CF ignored.

findings.title: WRITE_AT's INSIDE arm writes up to 511 bytes past the caller's buffer onto disk slack
findings.detail: The INSIDE arm hands dsk_read_chain_x [dskw_rem] whole sectors straight from ES:BX, and dskw_size32 rounds [dskw_rem] up for a partial final sector. On the loose path (end at or past the size) any count is allowed, so the bytes after the caller's buffer reach the slack. SPEC 18.4's binding 'No memory ever leaks past EOF' says the kernel never hands a foreign machine what sits after a package's buffer. The GROW arm keeps that rule by zero-filling through dskw_wone; this arm does not. SPEC 18.4.7.2 accepts the rounding ('nothing there to lose') without noting that the bytes are the caller's memory past its buffer, which 18.4.7.1 itself names as the hazard. With DOS.O88 as the caller, the leaked bytes are its window buffer, i.e. an earlier file's data: the classic DOS slack leak, inherited.
evidence: SPEC.md 18.4 'No memory ever leaks past EOF'
SPEC.md 18.4.7.2 'the transfer rounds up to a whole sector'
findings.recommendation: Route the final partial sector through dskw_wone with [dskw_clba] aimed at it, or amend 18.4's rule to name this arm as the exception.
findings.bytes_est: +25 .cold resident kern_big (kern_small has no INSIDE arm)
findings.prior_art: DOS leaked slack the same way; os8088's rule is stricter
findings.verify_note: Confirmed: dskw_size32 (:2727-2747) rounds [dskw_rem] up when the tail is non-zero, and the INSIDE arm passes [dskw_rem] sectors straight from [dskw_seg]:[dskw_src]. SPEC 18.4.7.2 (:38152-38157) permits the round-up; 18.4 (:34600-34604) forbids the leak. kern_small: the arm is %ifndef KERN_SMALL.

findings.title: DSKW_RT_MAX bounds the size of a tree, not the depth of a cycle
findings.detail: dskw_rtbody decrements the guard on every iteration, every file deleted included. A tree of 4,096 entries plus levels (an installed program tree on a 32MB partition) stops part-deleted with FERR_IO. A cycle is descent without removal, so re-arming the guard after each removal keeps cycle detection and lets any real tree finish. Also: the guard's 'jz .corrupt' leaves the volume chdir'd wherever the walk stood - it does not go through dskw_rt_go_home as .corrupt_home does.
evidence: kernel/diskw.inc:1142-1144 guard decremented each pass, jz .corrupt (not .corrupt_home)
kernel/diskw.inc:1023-1028 'A 1.44MB volume cannot legitimately need this many'
findings.recommendation: mov word [dskw_rt_guard], DSKW_RT_MAX after each successful removal (three sites: file, LFN slot, emptied folder - or one shared re-arm label), and send the guard's trip through .corrupt_home.
findings.bytes_est: +6 per re-arm site (6-18) plus 0 for the jump target, .cold resident kern_big
findings.verify_note: Confirmed the guard counts every iteration (:1142-1144). Correction: the loop has three removal arms (.loop's file delete, .lfn, .empty's rmbody), so a single 6-byte store needs a shared label; and the guard's jz .corrupt skips dskw_rt_go_home, leaving the current directory deep in the tree - added.

findings.title: kern_small's WRITE_AT stub answers CF=1 with AX = the caller's offset
findings.detail: dwf_dskw_write_at on kern_small enters at stc, below the mov ax, FERR_NAME its three neighbours fall through. The contract says AX = FERR_* on failure; the caller's offset low word is often 0, which reads as FERR_OK with CF=1.
findings.recommendation: Move the dwf_dskw_write_at label above mov ax, FERR_NAME.
findings.verify_note: Confirmed at diskw.inc:6805-6811: the label sits on 'stc' after 'mov ax, FERR_NAME'. Low reach: the comment says DOS.O88, the one caller, does not ship on the small disks.

findings.title: dskw_find matches the volume label, so its name cannot be used
findings.detail: Only attr&3Fh==0Fh entries (LFN) are skipped, so the volume label is matched. A file named like the label is refused FERR_PROT on write, and a folder FERR_EXIST on mkdir. DOS matches the label only for searches that ask for attribute 08h.
findings.recommendation: Replace 'and al,3Fh / cmp al,0Fh / je .next' with 'test al,08h / jnz .next', which skips both LFN and label entries. First grep that no caller uses dskw_find to locate the label on purpose.
findings.verify_note: Confirmed at :4407-4410; byte arithmetic (6 bytes -> 4) checks.

findings.title: The compression hint occupies dirent bytes NT, Linux, macOS and OS/2 interpret
findings.detail: +12 is NTRes = 5Ah/5Bh. Bits 3 and 4 are set, and NT/2000+, Linux vfat (default shortname=mixed) and macOS msdosfs read those bits as 'base and extension lower case'. So every packed file, which is every package on every shipped disk under PKGZ=lz4, lists in lower case on a modern host. +13 (CrtTimeTenth) gets U's high byte: up to 2s create-time skew, and values above 199 are invalid. +20 is the OS/2 and NT FASTFAT EA handle on FAT12/16. SPEC 20.14.1 calls these 'three bytes FAT12 and FAT16 leave free'. The hint is a cache with a sniff fallback, so moving it is read-safe.
evidence: SPEC.md:49252 'three bytes FAT12 and FAT16 leave free'
findings.recommendation: Choose a mark with bits 3 and 4 clear (40h-47h, A0h-A7h, ...); accept 5Ah/5Bh for one cycle in dskw_czknow and the listing's reader; switch tools/os88disk.py. Then decide, against a real NT CHKDSK, whether U may stay at +13/+20 or is learned from the 'CZ' header at open via dsk_peek_x, leaving a 1-bit flag.
findings.prior_art: GEOS kept metadata inside the file header, where no host strips or misreads it; os8088's 'CZ' header already does this
findings.verify_note: Confirmed 5Ah = 0101 1010b (bits 3 and 4 set); os88disk.py writes it for every packed file it is handed; SPEC 20.14.1 claims the bytes are free.

findings.title: Short names with bytes 80h-FFh, or a leading 05h, are listed but cannot be opened, deleted or renamed
findings.detail: dskw_char_x accepts only A-Z, 0-9 and dskw_syms. The FAT short-name set includes 80h-FFh (the OEM code page), and a name whose first character is E5h is stored as 05h. The listing synthesises such names, but every operation goes through dskw_name83 and answers FERR_NAME, so a file a DOS machine wrote is visible and untouchable.
findings.recommendation: Accept 80h-FFh in dskw_char_x (no upcase, as DOS did without COUNTRY) and map a leading E5h to 05h in dskw_name83.
findings.verify_note: Confirmed: dskw_char_x has no 80h-FFh arm; SPEC 18.4 'Names' states the 21h..7Eh choice deliberately, but calls it 'the FAT short-name set', which it is not.

findings.title: Subdirectories never grow: a kernel-made folder on a 512-byte-cluster volume holds 14 entries
findings.detail: When a subdirectory's chain ends with no free slot, every create answers FERR_DIRFULL. On 512-byte clusters (1.44MB, 1.2MB, the 360KB system disk) a kernel-made folder holds 14 entries after '.' and '..'; on 1KB clusters (720KB, the other 360KB disks) 30. SPEC (19.3.2) records the 14-entry limit and RunCPM's section (SPEC.md:133703-133709) records a save that failed on the glass because of it. DOS 2.0 grew subdirectories from day one. The pieces exist: mkdir already allocates and zeroes a directory cluster, and both slot users (dskw_commit and fcp_relink) go through dskw_find's no-slot exit.
evidence: SPEC.md:43108-43111 'which a directory never grows past'
findings.recommendation: dskw_dirgrow at dskw_find's no-slot exit for a subdirectory: alloc, zero (mkdir's loop factored out), flush, link the walker's last cluster to it, flush, publish its first sector as [dskw_fsec] with [dskw_fend]=1. A crash after the link leaves an empty extra cluster, which is harmless.
findings.prior_art: MS-DOS 2.0+ extends a directory by a zeroed cluster
findings.verify_note: Confirmed no growth path. Correction: the title said '1.44MB/720KB'; 720KB has 1KB clusters (30 entries). SPEC.md:43108-43111 is 19.3.2, the 360KB system disk at --spc 1.

findings.title: A whole-file write discovers FERR_FULL only after writing everything it could
findings.detail: dskw_wdata allocates one cluster per pass and finds a full disk at the first failing dskw_alloc, after writing every byte before it. On an XT that is seconds to minutes of floppy for a save that cannot land, followed on FAT16 by dw-2's leak. The kernel knows [dskw_rem] before the first sector, which DOS's incremental model never could.
findings.recommendation: Compare ceil(rem/spc) against a goal-bounded dsk_free_clus_x ([dsk_fcgoal] = the clusters needed, which already stops a FAT16 count early) before any data I/O and refuse FERR_FULL. On a floppy the count is CPU only (the whole FAT is the window); on a multi-window FAT16 it faults FAT windows in, i.e. it is disk I/O, so the goal bound is what keeps it cheap. A replace needs room for both copies (the old chain is held), so the needed count is the new chain's alone.
findings.bytes_est: +18-25 .cold resident (kern_small has no dsk_fcgoal), free if dw-14 lands
findings.prior_art: Mac File Manager Allocate/SetEOF; OS/2 HPFS preallocation
findings.verify_note: Confirmed no up-front check in dskw_wbody (:1520-1600). Correction: dsk_free_clus_x's FAT16 arm calls dsk_fat_ofs_x per FAT sector (disk.inc:6432-6490), which loads windows from disk on a FAT bigger than the window, so 'the count is CPU only' holds only for floppies; dsk_fcgoal (22.5.2.1) is the existing early stop to use.

findings.title: Allocate a contiguous run when the size is known
findings.detail: dskw_alloc is first-fit from the rover, one cluster per call, so a full disk fragments 'exactly the way DOS's did'. Each fragment is a separate transfer, and on a floppy also a seek of 100ms or more on the XT. A whole-file write and a grow both know N up front.
evidence: SPEC.md 18.4 'fragments exactly the way DOS's did'
kernel/fsck.inc:2800-2856 fsk_findrun (the same idea over a bitmap)
findings.recommendation: For dskw_wbody and the non-held grow, search the window once for the lowest free run of N clusters at or after the rover (FAT16: a repne scasw variant of .scan); fall back to first-fit.
findings.prior_art: Mac PBAllocContig and HFS clumps; GEOS VM files
findings.verify_note: Confirmed first-fit one-at-a-time (:4686-4790) and SPEC.md:34745-34746's sentence. The byte figure is an estimate, not measured; a FAT16 run that crosses windows needs its own handling.

findings.title: Defer the post-commit FAT flush (frees only) to gfx_unlock, the gate held streams already use
findings.detail: dskw_relold flushes FAT1 and FAT2 after every replace, delete, rmdir and truncate: two int 13h calls, about 0.8s per operation on the XT, and 100 calls for a 50-file rmtree. Dirt that is only frees is always safe to lose (lost clusters) and safe to reuse unflushed, because those clusters are unreachable on disk. The one real danger is a floppy swap. WRITE_SEQ already closes that hole by committing at gfx_unlock, 'every way the user can reach the drive'.
findings.recommendation: dskw_relold frees and leaves the range dirty under a dskw_lazy byte; dwsf_commit (gfx_unlock) and OSAPI_BATCH_END flush it. Park and the next write's flush behave as today. kern_small keeps the immediate flush. Mind dw-5: deferred dirt is exactly what dsk_fatw_park carries across a swap, so the gfx_unlock flush must land before any path that can park.
findings.prior_art: DOS FAT BUFFERS flushed at close/reset; SmartDrive write-behind; HFS lazy VBM/MDB (all deferred everything; this defers only droppable frees)
findings.verify_note: Confirmed relold always flushes and the comment gives the media-change reason (:962-970); the gfx_unlock commit for held streams exists (:3366-3372, :6798-6801).

findings.title: The rover resets at every navigation, and FAT12 allocation is three nested calls a cluster
findings.detail: disk_mount_x stores [dsk_rover]=2 unconditionally, including on the keepcwd remount every dsk_chdir performs. So the first save after any navigation re-walks the used front of the FAT. FAT16 has repne scasw; FAT12 keeps ~1,400 cycles a cluster, about 0.8s on a nearly full 1.44MB disk after every chdir.
evidence: kernel/disk.inc:4130-4140 rover reset beside the keepcwd branch
kernel/disk.inc:8258-8263 dsk_chdir_x is a keepcwd disk_mount_x
SPEC.md 18.4.10 'FAT12 ... keeps the loop', per-cluster cycle figure
findings.recommendation: Reset the rover only on the non-keepcwd arm: a hint, so a same-disk remount cannot make it wrong. Optionally add a FAT12 whole-window scan like dsk_free_clus_x's fast path.
findings.verify_note: Confirmed disk.inc:4130-4140 and dsk_chdir_x (:8258-8263).

findings.title: rmtree finds every file twice
findings.detail: dskw_rt_scan stages the entry and its location via dskw_hit. dskw_dbody_n83 then calls dskw_find, a second directory walk from entry 0 per file.
findings.recommendation: Enter the delete past its dskw_find (at the imgro and protection test) when dskw_raw is already staged.
findings.verify_note: Confirmed. The second walk usually ends in the same sector (the scan always finds the first live entry), so the cost is CPU and a re-read of that sector, not a long walk.

findings.title: fsck's FILEnnnn.CHK number uses an 8-bit multiply and wraps at 10,000 into duplicates
findings.detail: fsk_lost_num multiplies AL by 10, so any existing number of 2,560 or more is misparsed. fsk_save writes four digits of P_CHKN, so 10,000 becomes FILE0000, a duplicate name. Neither can collide in a 224/512-entry root in practice, but both are wrong.
findings.recommendation: Use a 16-bit multiply; saturate P_CHKN at 9,999 and treat the cap as a full root (free the chain), as DOS CHKDSK stops at FILE9999.
findings.verify_note: Confirmed: 'mul dh' is AL*DH, so a three-digit prefix of 256 or more is truncated before the fourth digit.

findings.title: Taking the terminator in a sector's last slot trusts the next sector to be zero
findings.detail: dskw_ent_store and fsk_save write no new end marker when the taken 00 slot is the sector's last, on the claim that the next sector 'has never been written and is already 00'. That holds for every directory DOS or os8088 makes. On a foreign or hostile disk, non-zero bytes past the terminator would become live entries.
findings.recommendation: Record only: a fix costs a second sector RMW in 1 case of 16, and every reader already treats entries as hostile.
findings.verify_note: Confirmed at both sites.

findings.title: Pop runs and refusal tails shared across 1,000+ lines, held together by prose
findings.detail: dskw_find.out/.pdi/.psi/.pdx is the epilogue of six routines with matching push orders. More than ten 'X.out equ neighbour.ret' relays exist, and refusals jump into other bodies' labels (dskw_wbody.prot, dskw_rdata.corrupt, dskw_nbody.badarg, dskw_mkbody.exists). One reordered push in dskw_find silently breaks five callers.
findings.recommendation: A DSKW_PUSH6/DSKW_POP6 macro pair that defines the order once, used by every routine that joins the shared run.
findings.verify_note: Spot-checked :1295 (dskw_rt_scan -> dskw_find.out) and :4790 (dskw_alloc -> dskw_find.pdx).

findings.title: Two 'same question, two predicates' pairs: LFN detection and mounted-image detection
findings.detail: dskw_find detects LFN with attr&3Fh==0Fh; rmtree with attr==0Fh exactly, so an LFN slot with high attribute bits makes rmtree delete it as a file and stop FERR_NOENT. The defragmenter skips *.IMG by name, while dskw_imgro asks the claim table by cluster, which is the real fact.
findings.recommendation: Mask in rmtree; let fsk_defent ask dsk_img_next by cluster, which also lets it move an unmounted .IMG.
findings.verify_note: Confirmed all four sites.

findings.title: WRITE_SEQ's single kernel-wide stream record thrashes under two concurrent streams
findings.detail: dws_rec is one record keyed by [dsk_mgen]. Two streams (an FTP upload and a DOS COPY, or two FTPD sessions) make each other's tokens cold every call. Each call then commits and falls back to APPEND: a name lookup plus a whole-chain walk (DISK-CPU-PLAN 6), O(n^2) over the file. DOS's SFT had FILES= entries, and READ_SEQ already made its cursor the caller's.
findings.recommendation: Make the committed position caller-held (an ES:DI cursor like READ_SEQ's) while the HOLD stays the kernel's, one at a time.
findings.prior_art: MS-DOS SFT, one entry per open handle
findings.verify_note: Spot-checked: one record, keyed by [dsk_mgen] (:3355-3364).

findings.title: No 'volume dirty' mark while a hold or deferred dirt is pending
findings.detail: A kept hold (WSQF_KEEP) can outlive callbacks on a fixed disk, and so would dw-15's deferred frees. FAT16 reserves FAT[1] bit 15 (ClnShutBitMask) for this. AmigaOS ran the disk-validator on an unvalidated volume; HPFS had a dirty flag. Combined with System Check's AUTOSTRT link, a set bit at boot could trigger an unattended check.
findings.recommendation: Record. The cost is one FAT-sector write per transition.
findings.prior_art: FAT16 ClnShutBitMask (Win95/NT); AmigaOS disk-validator; HPFS dirty flag
findings.verify_note: Low-severity record item; not re-verified beyond WSQF_KEEP's existence (:3385).

findings.title: Delete and rename orphan a host's LFN entries
findings.detail: The scan passes over LFN entries, so deleting or renaming a host-named file leaves its LFN run behind. Windows 95+ deletes the preceding LFN run with a matching checksum, and ScanDisk and fsck.fat report orphans otherwise.
evidence: SPEC.md 18.4 'leaves that name's LFN entries orphaned'
findings.recommendation: Record: mark the contiguous preceding 0Fh entries E5h in the same sector.
findings.verify_note: SPEC.md:34641-34646 says it as quoted.

doc_fixes.old_text:
**Rollback.** Any failure *before* the commit reloads the FAT snapshot from
disk (`dskw_refat`, one `disk_read` of `dsk_fatsz` sectors) and clears the
dirty range, so a partially allocated chain never survives in RAM to be
flushed by a later, unrelated operation.
doc_fixes.new_text:
**Rollback.** Any failure *before* the commit invalidates the FAT window and
clears the dirty range (`dskw_refat`, no I/O: the next access faults a clean
window in off the disk), so a partially allocated chain never survives in
RAM to be flushed by a later, unrelated operation. An eviction may already
have flushed part of that chain (§18.8), which costs lost clusters, never a
cross-link.
doc_fixes.why: dskw_refat (diskw.inc:5002-5025) stores 0xFFFF/0 into three words and does no I/O; its header states the eviction caveat.

doc_fixes.old_text:
**What this deliberately does not do.** No paths (a name is resolved in the
current directory and nowhere else), no *recursive* directory removal —
`dskw_rmdir` (§18.6) takes an empty folder and refuses anything else, so
emptying a subtree is the user's job one level at a time — no append or seek, no
truncate-in-place, no FAT32, no volume-label editing, no timestamp
preservation across a rewrite, and no attempt to defragment: chains are
allocated first-fit from the rover, so a full disk fragments exactly the
way DOS's did.
